a: Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of deviation from rational judgment, caused by the brain's use of mental shortcuts (heuristics) to process information quickly. Common biases include: confirmation bias (favoring information that confirms existing beliefs), anchoring bias (relying too heavily on the first piece of information encountered), availability heuristic (overestimating the likelihood of easily recalled events), Dunning-Kruger effect (unskilled individuals overestimating their ability), hindsight bias (seeing past events as predictable), bandwagon effect (doing something because others do it), and sunk cost fallacy (continuing an endeavor because of past investment). These biases were extensively studied by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, who won the Nobel Prize for their work on prospect theory and behavioral economics. Awareness of cognitive biases can help improve decision-making.
